title: The Arabian Nights Entertainments
author: Andrew Lang (editor and adapter, after Antoine Galland)
estimatedTime: About 8 hours in all; each tale takes minutes to an hour
openingText: The chronicles of the ancient dynasty of the Sassanidae, which ruled for about four hundred years from Persia to the borders of China and even beyond the great river Ganges, record the praises of one king of this line, who was held to be the finest ruler of his day.
about:
A sultan who has decided to marry a new wife each day and have her put to death at dawn meets Scheherazade, the vizier’s daughter, who begins a story and leaves it unfinished. This selection, edited by Andrew Lang in 1898, translates stories from Antoine Galland’s French version of the Nights. Lang shortened the stories in places and left out most of the verse.

The tales nest inside one another. A merchant is saved by the stories of three old men, three princes tell their own histories, and Sindbad the Sailor recounts seven voyages to an audience that includes a porter. Genies, caliphs and viziers appear alongside fishermen, tailors and merchants. Aladdin and the Wonderful Lamp, the Enchanted Horse and Ali Cogia are here, together with some less familiar stories.

A short preface by Lang explains how the book came to Europe. You can read each tale as a separate story or follow the thread of the frame story from the beginning.

whyItMatters.title: A story keeps the storyteller alive
whyItMatters.body: Scheherazade tells her stories to stay alive, and the sultan keeps postponing her sentence to hear how each one ends. The frame makes storytelling an act with consequences. Within the tales, characters likewise save themselves by telling the right story at the right moment. The idea that a good narrative can buy time is easy to recognise in modern serial entertainment.

whyItMatters.title: Tales sit inside other tales
whyItMatters.body: The Story of the Merchant and the Genie contains the tales of three old men, and the Story of the Three Calenders contains the histories of three princes. Each narrator speaks for himself, and each listener is changed by what he hears. The layering lets one book hold many voices and many settings. Streaming series and podcasts use nested stories for the same reason.

whyItMatters.title: Wonder and danger share the same roads
whyItMatters.body: Sindbad’s voyages bring him jewels and also shipwreck, giant birds and the Old Man of the Sea. Aladdin’s lamp makes him rich and puts his life at risk. The tales rarely separate marvel from peril or fortune from loss. Readers who know only the cartoons will find the originals a good deal more ambiguous.

angleCards.title: Follow the frame story
angleCards.text: Keep track of how Scheherazade’s tales interrupt, postpone and answer the sultan’s decision.
angleCards.angleObjective: I’m reading The Arabian Nights Entertainments to follow how the storytelling frame shapes the tales inside it.

angleCards.title: Track the nested narrators
angleCards.text: Notice who tells each story, who listens and what changes when a tale is told inside another.
angleCards.angleObjective: I’m reading The Arabian Nights Entertainments to examine how stories within stories change what each narrator and listener understands.

angleCards.title: Compare the sea and the city
angleCards.text: Set Sindbad’s voyages beside the stories set in Baghdad, and compare what each treats as danger and as reward.
angleCards.angleObjective: I’m reading The Arabian Nights Entertainments to compare the adventures at sea with the stories set in cities.

angleCards.title: Read Lang’s choices
angleCards.text: Read the preface, then notice what a nineteenth-century editor kept, shortened and removed from Galland’s version.
angleCards.angleObjective: I’m reading The Arabian Nights Entertainments to understand how Galland and Lang shaped what English readers know as the Nights.
